title: China Raises Rare Earth Stakes as Datacenters Brace for November Curbs, While Apple and Nvidia Reportedly Team Up on AI Servers
subhead: Beijing's escalating export controls on rare earths and critical minerals are now pointed squarely at the AI buildout, just as Apple reportedly plans a return to the server market using Nvidia's NVLink interconnect — and as Washington prepares for a Trump-Xi summit where AI and export controls top the agenda.

sections.heading: Rare Earth and Critical Minerals: China's Curbs Tighten on the AI Buildout
sections.body: China has tightened its rare earth export controls, expanding restrictions on processing technology and unauthorised overseas cooperation, and spelling out an intention to limit exports to overseas defence and semiconductor users, according to a Reuters report picked up by Yahoo Finance. The Register reports that datacenters face a direct hit from the expanded curbs, with the clock running out on an escalated licensing regime. Fastmarkets notes China's looming November export controls will test the country's own refining and recycling ambitions, while S&P Global compiles the weight the curbs now place on global critical minerals supply.
sections.whyItMatters: Rare earths and the processing know-how behind them underpin the magnets and specialty materials in AI data-center equipment, so this moves the export-control fight from advanced chips into the raw and processed materials layer of the AI supply chain.

sections.heading: Compute Sovereignty: Apple Reportedly Turns to Nvidia's NVLink for New AI Servers
sections.body: The Information reports that Apple is considering a return to the server market and has talked with Nvidia about using its network interconnect technology. TrendForce and Tom's Hardware amplify the report: Apple's custom M8 Ultra chips would be paired with Nvidia NVLink for a 2029 data center push — a notable thaw in a historically bitter rivalry between the two companies. Separately, Apple and Intel have circled closer, with CNBC reporting earlier this year that Intel began production of its most-advanced chip, inching toward a possible Apple deal.
sections.whyItMatters: A US hardware champion building its own AI servers with its own silicon, while relying on Nvidia's interconnect for scale, would reshape the competitive map — and keep more of the AI compute stack onshore in American hands.

sections.heading: US-China AI Diplomacy: The Trump-Xi Summit Looms With Export Controls in View
sections.body: The upcoming Trump-Xi summit in Washington will put AI on the agenda, with 'Track Two' talks already buzzing, NPR reports. The World Economic Forum lays out what to expect from the meeting, and the Council on Foreign Relations argues the US-China AI race is changing the stakes for Taiwan. On the policy periphery, the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) argues in a fresh analysis that America must expand AI export controls amid talks with China, while a Carnegie Endowment piece surveys the geopolitical debates over controlling cloud compute — the software layer of AI beyond hardware chips.
sections.whyItMatters: With a leaders' meeting days away, the core question is whether AI and export controls get negotiated or stay contested — and think tanks on both the expansion and restraint sides are already framing the terms.

sections.heading: Semiconductor Sanctions and Enforcement in Practice
sections.body: Beyond Washington, enforcement and re-export dynamics are in focus. Australia's International Affairs notes the MATCH Act and the limits of allied semiconductor controls, where cooperation depends on allies that control critical technologies but do not always share identical economic interests. Trade press coverage this week also re-surfaces how US curbs on advanced computing and semiconductor manufacturing have reshaped China's tech scene, with the South China Morning Post charting years of 'attack the chokepoints' export control policy. US prosecutors separately pressed their racketeering case against Huawei in New York, accusing the company of a 'far-reaching criminal scheme' spanning decades, per the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists.
sections.whyItMatters: The US export-control regime now depends as much on allied compliance and enforcement as on the rules themselves, and the Huawei trial keeps a spotlight on how those rules are put into practice.

sections.heading: Space and Orbital Power: Starship Slips to Sept. 28, Cable Threats Loom
sections.body: SpaceX has pushed the next Starship launch back to Sept. 28, a six-day delay for the megarocket's first orbital attempt, Space.com reports, after the company had flagged Flight 14 details on its own site. On the threat side, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies warns that Russia is practicing attacks on undersea cables in the Arctic, with consequences that could reach into the space domain as orbital constellations increasingly carry resilience hopes for global connectivity.
sections.whyItMatters: Orbital capacity and undersea resilience are converging into a single connectivity-strategy question: how much redundancy governments can buy, and from whom, as both launch slots and cable routes become strategic assets.

sections.heading: Cyber Power: State-Sponsored Infrastructure Threats in Focus
sections.body: Industrial Cyber reports that a Congressional Research Service finding describes Iranian state-sponsored hackers exploiting Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet flaws to access US infrastructure networks. Meanwhile, the broader picture on critical infrastructure remains contested: earlier coverage flagged US and allied warnings about Russian cyberattacks targeting routers, and government admissions that water-system cyberattacks were worse than first reported. None of these are new incidents this week, but they keep the exposure of US networks to state-backed intrusion front and center.
sections.whyItMatters: The steady drumbeat of state-sponsored activity against infrastructure shows the threat is persistent and evolving, even when no single headline incident breaks a given week.

bottomLine: China hardened its rare earth and critical minerals export controls with defence and semiconductor users squarely in its sights, and November looms as the next escalation point — a move that drags the AI buildout's raw-materials layer into the US-China tech fight. At the same time, Apple reportedly plans its own AI servers on its own silicon with Nvidia's NVLink, a US-on-US alignment that keeps more compute onshore. With the Trump-Xi summit days away and think tanks like CNAS already urging expanded AI export controls, the week ahead may decide whether AI is negotiated or further weaponised. Huawei's racketeering trial, SpaceX's delayed Starship attempt, and persistent state-sponsored cyber activity round out a week heavy on escalation and light on resolution.
